cards.statement: Angular resolves a relative styleUrl from the workspace root.
cards.explanation: Angular resolves styleUrl relative to the directory containing the component file.
cards.misconception: Workspace-relative component styles.

cards.statement: Since Angular v19, @Component defaults to standalone: false.
cards.explanation: Components are standalone by default. A component declared in an NgModule uses standalone: false.
cards.misconception: NgModule declaration is the default.

cards.statement: Angular creates a separate component instance for each matching template element.
cards.explanation: Repeated uses of a component selector produce distinct instances with their own component state.

cards.statement: Angular replaces a component's host element with the component's rendered view.
cards.explanation: Angular keeps the host element and renders the component's template inside it.
cards.misconception: The view replaces its host.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends host metadata over @HostBinding and @HostListener.
cards.explanation: The host property centralizes host bindings; the decorators remain for backwards compatibility.

cards.statement: Angular appends ng-content fallback content after the matching projected children.
cards.explanation: Angular displays a slot's fallback content when that slot receives no matching child content.
cards.misconception: Fallback content accompanies matches.

cards.statement: Placing ng-content inside @if postpones projected content creation until the condition becomes truthy.
cards.explanation: Angular creates projected content even when its ng-content placeholder is hidden. The guide advises against conditional ng-content.
cards.misconception: Conditional slots defer content creation.

cards.statement: Angular uses ViewEncapsulation.Emulated when a component leaves encapsulation unspecified.
cards.explanation: Angular scopes component styles by adding generated attributes to template elements and style selectors.

cards.statement: ViewEncapsulation.Emulated isolates component elements from matching global style rules.
cards.explanation: Global styles can still affect elements inside a component using Emulated encapsulation.
cards.misconception: Emulated encapsulation blocks global styles.

cards.statement: Angular's style guide prefers protected for template-only component members.
cards.explanation: Using protected keeps template helpers out of the component class's public API.

cards.statement: Angular writes an empty string to an attr. binding's attribute when its value is null.
cards.explanation: A null attribute-binding value makes Angular remove the attribute.
cards.misconception: Null becomes an empty attribute.

source.title: Binding dynamic text, properties and attributes

cards.statement: Angular's style guide prefers NgClass over class bindings for template styling.
cards.explanation: The style guide prefers built-in class bindings over NgClass.
cards.misconception: NgClass is the recommended choice.

cards.statement: Angular exposes the triggering event as $event inside a template event listener.
cards.explanation: A listener passes $event to a handler when that handler needs the event's details.

cards.statement: Angular writes two-way binding with parentheses inside square brackets, as in [(value)].
cards.explanation: The [(...)] form combines the property's binding with the corresponding event binding.

cards.statement: Angular assigns an unqualified #ref on a component element to that element's native DOM node.
cards.explanation: On an Angular component, an unqualified template reference holds the component instance.
cards.misconception: Component references target native nodes.

cards.statement: Angular keeps an @let variable current as the declaration's template expression changes.
cards.explanation: An @let declaration follows its expression like a binding instead of preserving an initial snapshot.

cards.statement: In `ready ? a : b | format`, Angular pipes the entire conditional result through format.
cards.explanation: Angular reads `ready ? a : b | format` as `ready ? a : (b | format)` because a pipe binds more tightly than a ternary.
cards.misconception: Ternaries bind more tightly than pipes.

cards.statement: Angular template expressions support parseInt as a built-in global function.
cards.explanation: The supported globals are undefined and $any. Expose other functions through the component when needed.
cards.misconception: JavaScript globals exist in templates.

cards.statement: Angular template expressions support arrow functions that use an expression body.
cards.explanation: Template arrow functions use an expression after =>; block-bodied arrow functions are rejected.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, template optional chaining yields undefined for a nullish receiver.
cards.explanation: Angular's template ?. operator returns undefined when its receiver is null or undefined.

cards.statement: An @if as alias holds the condition's evaluated result inside the rendered block.
cards.explanation: The alias exposes the expression result, such as a user object, for reuse within that branch.

cards.statement: An @for block supports a Set of items as the collection it renders in a template.
cards.explanation: @for accepts JavaScript iterables, including Set, while Angular optimizes Array iteration.

cards.statement: Angular requires a track expression when compiling an @for block.
cards.explanation: A missing track expression is a compilation error because Angular needs a key for associating items with views.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends track $index for lists that reorder their items.
cards.explanation: The guide recommends a unique item property for changing collections; $index suits static collections.
cards.misconception: Index tracking suits reordering.

cards.statement: An @for view is recreated when its tracked key changes on the same object.
cards.explanation: When the object reference stays the same, @for updates the view's bindings instead of recreating the view.
cards.misconception: Changed keys recreate retained objects.

cards.statement: An @for track expression accepts the loop's contextual $count value.
cards.explanation: Track expressions use the item, $index or its alias, and component members. $count is outside that permitted context.
cards.misconception: Track accepts every loop local.

cards.statement: An @for block supports break for ending template iteration early.
cards.explanation: Angular's @for block rejects break statements; express the desired collection in the data supplied to the block.
cards.misconception: Template loops accept break.

cards.statement: Angular uses == to compare an @switch value with its case expressions.
cards.explanation: @switch compares each case expression with the switch value using ===.
cards.misconception: Switch cases coerce compared values.

cards.statement: Consecutive @case blocks can select a shared content block inside an @switch.
cards.explanation: List consecutive cases before one body to render that body for any of those matching values.

cards.statement: Exhaustive @switch checks support a signal call as the switch expression.
cards.explanation: Exhaustiveness checks rely on narrowing a variable. A direct signal read as the switch expression does not support that check.
cards.misconception: Signal calls support union exhaustiveness.

cards.statement: In Angular v20 and later, NgIf is deprecated in favor of the @if block.
cards.explanation: NgIf remains present in Angular v22 with a deprecation notice directing users to @if.
cards.volatilityNote: NgIf remains in v22, but its API declares intent to remove it in a future major release.

cards.statement: Angular lazily loads an NgModule-declared component used directly inside @defer.
cards.explanation: Direct NgModule-based dependencies of @defer load eagerly.
cards.misconception: NgModule dependencies are deferrable.

cards.statement: Referencing a deferred component's class in a same-file ViewChild query makes its code load eagerly.
cards.explanation: Same-file ViewChild class references defeat that dependency's @defer splitting.

cards.statement: Angular eagerly loads the dependencies used in an @defer block's @loading content.
cards.explanation: @loading content belongs to the eager bundle.

cards.statement: The after option of @loading postpones Angular's deferred dependency fetch.
cards.explanation: @loading's after postpones its display, rather than fetching.
cards.misconception: Delayed fetching.

cards.statement: Angular starts a @placeholder minimum timer when that placeholder first renders.
cards.explanation: A placeholder's minimum display interval begins with its initial render.

cards.statement: Angular uses on viewport as the default trigger for an unconfigured @defer block.
cards.explanation: An unconfigured @defer starts loading when the browser becomes idle.
cards.misconception: Viewport is the default trigger.

cards.statement: For on viewport, Angular watches the @placeholder element by default.
cards.explanation: @defer uses its placeholder as the implicit viewport target.

cards.statement: Angular can use a multi-root @placeholder as the implicit on interaction target.
cards.explanation: An implicit interaction target requires one placeholder root element.
cards.misconception: Multiple trigger roots.

cards.statement: A @defer when condition restores the placeholder after changing back to false.
cards.explanation: @defer's when activates once; subsequent falsy values leave content displayed.
cards.misconception: Reversible condition trigger.

cards.statement: With `on interaction; prefetch on idle`, the @defer placeholder stays after the idle prefetch.
cards.explanation: A prefetch trigger only downloads the block's JavaScript. The placeholder stays until the main on or when trigger fires, here a user interaction with the placeholder.

cards.statement: With HMR active, Angular waits for @defer triggers before fetching their chunks.
cards.explanation: HMR fetches @defer chunks eagerly, bypassing configured triggers.
cards.misconception: HMR preserves lazy fetching.
cards.volatilityNote: HMR's eager chunk-fetching behavior is tooling behavior that may change in later releases.

cards.statement: A barrel import can keep a deferred component in the application's main bundle.
cards.explanation: Barrel exports may defeat @defer chunk splitting.
cards.volatilityNote: Lazy chunk splitting through barrels depends on compiler and bundler behavior that may change.

cards.statement: A WritableSignal's update() callback receives the signal's current value.
cards.explanation: Angular passes the current signal value to update(), and stores the callback's result as the new value.

cards.statement: A WritableSignal's asReadonly() also freezes the nested objects stored in the signal's value.
cards.explanation: asReadonly() exposes a read-only signal API while leaving nested objects mutable.
cards.misconception: Read-only signals freeze their contents.

cards.statement: A computed signal evaluates its derivation when a consumer first reads its value.
cards.explanation: Angular delays the first computed derivation until its value is read.

cards.statement: A computed signal tracks signals referenced in a branch its latest derivation skips.
cards.explanation: Angular tracks the signals actually read during the most recent computed derivation.
cards.misconception: Computed dependencies come from static references.

cards.statement: Angular signals compare old and new values with Object.is when equal is unspecified.
cards.explanation: The default equality check determines whether Angular treats a signal value as changed.

cards.statement: An effect tracks a signal read after an await as a dependency of that effect.
cards.explanation: Angular's reactive context tracks synchronous reads; a read after await falls outside that context.
cards.misconception: Reactive tracking continues across await.

cards.statement: A linkedSignal computation with an explicit source can inspect its previous linked value.
cards.explanation: The optional previous object exposes previous.value, letting the computation preserve earlier linked state.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22.1, linkedSignal uses its custom set callback to derive source-driven updates.
cards.explanation: Source changes use computation. The custom set callback handles explicit set() and update() writes.
cards.misconception: Custom set handles reactive derivation.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends computed or linkedSignal over effect for propagating signal state.
cards.explanation: The guide recommends deriving signal state with computed or linkedSignal rather than copying it between signals in an effect.

cards.statement: An effect's onCleanup callback runs after its next execution finishes.
cards.explanation: Angular invokes an effect's registered cleanup before the next execution begins.
cards.misconception: Cleanup follows the replacement execution.

cards.statement: An effect created in a root-provided service's constructor outlives the component that injected the service.
cards.explanation: Effects created while a root-provided service is instantiated are root effects: Angular destroys them with the application, or when code calls destroy() on the returned EffectRef.

cards.statement: toSignal subscribes to its Observable when a consumer first reads the resulting signal.
cards.explanation: Calling toSignal creates the subscription immediately, even before the resulting signal is read.
cards.misconception: Subscription waits for signal consumption.

cards.statement: A resource calls its loader when the params computation returns undefined.
cards.explanation: Undefined params put the resource in idle state and prevent that loader invocation.
cards.misconception: Undefined params reach the loader.

cards.statement: If a resource's params change mid-load, Angular aborts the loader's abortSignal.
cards.explanation: Angular aborts an outstanding load when params change. A loader that passes abortSignal to fetch or a similar API cancels the obsolete request.

cards.statement: A resource clears its previous value while reload() fetches a replacement value.
cards.explanation: During reloading, value() retains the previously loaded value until the replacement arrives.
cards.misconception: Reloading clears existing data.

cards.statement: A resource's hasValue() guard protects a value() read from throwing in the error state.
cards.explanation: When a resource is in error state, value() throws and hasValue() returns false.

cards.statement: Calling set() on a ResourceRef changes its status to resolved after the local write.
cards.explanation: A local set() or update() write puts the resource in local status.
cards.misconception: Local writes count as resolved loads.

cards.statement: For plain User objects, resource's stream option accepts a callback returning Promise<User>.
cards.explanation: stream returns a Signal<ResourceStreamItem<User>> or a PromiseLike resolving to that signal. The signal carries changing value or error entries.
cards.misconception: A stream resolves plain data like a loader.

cards.statement: rxResource supports a loader option that returns an Observable as its data source.
cards.explanation: Configure rxResource with stream: a function returning the Observable used as its data source.
cards.misconception: The Observable factory uses the loader option.

cards.statement: Requests from httpResource traverse the configured HttpClient interceptor chain.
cards.explanation: httpResource builds its requests on HttpClient, so configured interceptors participate in them.

cards.statement: A resource configured with defaultValue: [] returns undefined during its initial load.
cards.explanation: While initial loading is pending, value() returns the configured defaultValue, such as [], until a loaded value replaces it.
cards.misconception: Initial loading hides the configured fallback.

cards.statement: httpResource parses the response body as JSON unless a variant like httpResource.text is used.
cards.explanation: JSON parsing is the httpResource default. httpResource.text, httpResource.blob and httpResource.arrayBuffer give a string, a Blob or an ArrayBuffer in value() instead.

cards.statement: An input declared with input<number>() includes undefined in its value type.
cards.explanation: Angular includes undefined because this input declaration supplies no initial value.

cards.statement: Angular defers a missing input.required template-binding error until component creation.
cards.explanation: Angular reports a missing required input binding during the template's build-time checks.
cards.misconception: Required template bindings are checked at creation.

cards.statement: An input transform's return type determines which values a template may bind.
cards.explanation: Angular checks bound values against the transform function's parameter type.
cards.misconception: Binding types follow the transformed result.

cards.statement: booleanAttribute converts the string "false" to true when Angular transforms an input.
cards.explanation: Angular's booleanAttribute explicitly converts the literal string "false" to the boolean false.
cards.misconception: Any present string becomes true.

cards.statement: contentChildren searches a component's direct content children by default.
cards.explanation: The default contentChildren query checks direct children; set descendants: true to search more deeply.

cards.statement: A model input's two-way binding can accept the parent's writable signal instance as its target.
cards.explanation: Bind the writable signal itself, such as [(value)]="volume", so model updates flow back into that signal.

cards.statement: A model input supports a transform option for converting values received from its parent.
cards.explanation: Angular's model input API provides no transform option for incoming values.
cards.misconception: Model inputs share input transforms.

cards.statement: Events emitted through output() bubble from the component host through the DOM tree.
cards.explanation: Angular output events reach their bound listeners rather than bubbling through the DOM.
cards.misconception: Angular outputs bubble like native events.

cards.statement: Angular automatically ends programmatic subscriptions to an output() when its owning component is destroyed.
cards.explanation: An output() returns an OutputEmitterRef. Angular drops the listeners registered with its subscribe() when the owning directive or component is destroyed, so no manual unsubscribe is needed.

cards.statement: Reading a required viewChild query throws after @if removes its matching element.
cards.explanation: A required query raises an error when read while its result is missing, including after conditional content disappears.

cards.statement: viewChild searches inside the templates of child components for a matching result.
cards.explanation: A view query stays within its owner's template; Angular queries stop at component boundaries.
cards.misconception: View queries descend into child templates.

cards.statement: A field initializer in an Angular DI-created component runs in an injection context.
cards.explanation: Angular makes inject() available while it initializes fields of a component it creates through DI.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, @Service() supplies a root singleton for its decorated service class.
cards.explanation: The root injector shares the service instance supplied by @Service() across its consumers.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, @Service() resolves dependency tokens from constructor parameters.
cards.explanation: A @Service class obtains injected dependencies with inject(), rather than constructor parameter injection.
cards.misconception: Service accepts constructor-based DI.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, @Service({autoProvided: false}) supports manual provision in a component's providers.
cards.explanation: autoProvided: false leaves registration to a providers array, allowing the service to be scoped to that component.

cards.statement: Angular provides a factory-backed InjectionToken at root when providedIn is omitted.
cards.explanation: A token factory supplies its own provider, whose default scope is the root injector.

cards.statement: A useExisting provider makes a second token resolve to the same dependency instance.
cards.explanation: useExisting aliases an existing provider's value instead of constructing a replacement instance.

cards.statement: A component that lists a root-provided service in its providers reuses the root instance.
cards.explanation: Listing the class creates a separate component-scoped service instance, tied to that component's lifetime.
cards.misconception: Component class providers reuse root instances.

cards.statement: For a component dependency, Angular checks EnvironmentInjector before an ancestor ElementInjector.
cards.explanation: Angular walks the ElementInjector hierarchy, including ancestors, before trying the EnvironmentInjector hierarchy.
cards.misconception: Environment providers outrank ancestor element providers.

cards.statement: Angular returns undefined for an optional inject() call whose provider lookup fails.
cards.explanation: With optional: true, inject() returns null when Angular fails to find the requested provider.
cards.misconception: Optional lookup failure produces undefined.

cards.statement: With self: true, inject() treats each directive on one element as a separate provider scope.
cards.explanation: Angular applies self at injector level; directives on one element share that ElementInjector.
cards.misconception: Self means a separate scope for each directive.

cards.statement: A component's viewProviders exposes its service to components projected into that component.
cards.explanation: Angular excludes projected content from the provider visibility established by viewProviders.
cards.misconception: Projected content receives viewProviders.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, injectAsync() requires an auto-provided service for lazy injection.
cards.explanation: A service declared with @Injectable({providedIn: 'root'}) satisfies injectAsync's automatic provision requirement.

cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, applications use zoneless change detection by default.
cards.explanation: Angular schedules checks from framework notifications rather than relying on ZoneJS to observe asynchronous activity.

cards.statement: In a zoneless application, NgZone.onStable emits after Angular finishes change detection.
cards.explanation: NgZone.onStable does not emit in a zoneless application. Code waiting on it needs a different completion signal.
cards.misconception: NgZone.onStable continues to report rendering completion in zoneless applications.

cards.statement: During server rendering, PendingTasks.run() delays serialization until its async callback completes.
cards.explanation: PendingTasks.run() registers its async callback as work that keeps the application unstable until it finishes.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular selects OnPush for components whose changeDetection metadata is unset.
cards.explanation: A component with no explicit changeDetection setting uses OnPush. The strategy controls when Angular checks its subtree.

cards.statement: Changing a field of an object input in place by itself triggers a check of an OnPush child.
cards.explanation: Angular compares input values with Object.is. An in-place edit preserves the input reference and does not itself trigger an OnPush check.
cards.misconception: Angular treats nested edits to an input object as a new input value.

cards.statement: Angular marks an OnPush component for checking when a signal value read in its template changes.
cards.explanation: A template signal read registers a dependency on that component. A changed signal value marks the component for a subsequent check.

cards.statement: Angular invokes the first ngOnChanges after ngOnInit when a component has bound inputs.
cards.explanation: During initialization, Angular invokes the first ngOnChanges before ngOnInit, letting the hook react to the initial input changes.
cards.misconception: The initialization hook precedes the first input-change hook.

cards.statement: With Eager change detection, changing a non-signal bound field in ngAfterViewInit passes Angular's dev-mode check.
cards.explanation: In development mode Angular rechecks bindings after each change detection run, so a bound value changed in ngAfterViewInit throws ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError. Set initial values in the constructor or ngOnInit.
cards.misconception: ngAfterViewInit is a safe place to synchronously change a bound field.

cards.statement: Angular runs cleanup registered on a component's injected DestroyRef when that component is destroyed.
cards.explanation: A DestroyRef injected in a component follows that component's lifetime. Its onDestroy method registers callbacks for teardown.

cards.statement: Angular executes afterNextRender callbacks during server rendering after producing the page's HTML.
cards.explanation: afterNextRender callbacks execute in the browser; Angular skips them during server rendering and build-time prerendering.
cards.misconception: Server rendering invokes afterNextRender once its HTML is ready.

cards.statement: Angular runs the write phase of afterNextRender before its read phase for layout measurements.
cards.explanation: Separating DOM writes from subsequent reads controls their order and helps avoid repeated layout work.

cards.statement: Angular ranks matching route paths by specificity before choosing an entry from the Routes array.
cards.explanation: Angular tests routes in array order and selects the first match. Place specific paths ahead of broader paths.
cards.misconception: The router sorts route definitions by specificity during matching.

cards.statement: A loadComponent loader can read its route's providers through inject() while the loader runs.
cards.explanation: The router invokes the loader in the current route's injection context, giving synchronous inject() calls access to that route's dependencies.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends eager loading for an application's primary landing pages.
cards.explanation: The loading guide recommends making primary landing pages available in the initial bundle while considering lazy loading for other pages.

cards.statement: Angular waits for a guard's Observable to complete before using its emitted navigation decision.
cards.explanation: The router uses the first value emitted by a guard's Observable and then unsubscribes, rather than waiting for completion.
cards.misconception: A guard decision stays pending until its Observable completes.

cards.statement: Angular continues looking for a matching route when a canMatch guard returns false.
cards.explanation: A false canMatch result rejects that route candidate while allowing route matching to continue with other candidates.

cards.statement: Angular activates a routed component before its ResolveFn supplies the initial resolved data.
cards.explanation: The router waits for the resolver's data before activating the route, so the component starts with its resolved data available.
cards.misconception: Initial resolvers load their data after the routed component activates.

cards.statement: Angular starts parent and child route resolvers concurrently during the same navigation.
cards.explanation: Nested route resolvers run from parent to child. Child resolvers start after the parent data resolves and can use that data.
cards.misconception: Parent and child resolver work starts in parallel.

cards.statement: withComponentInputBinding preserves an input's previous value when its matching route-state key disappears.
cards.explanation: The router sets an input to undefined when no matching route-state key exists, clearing stale values such as removed query parameters.
cards.misconception: Route input binding leaves a previous value in place when its source key disappears.

cards.statement: withComponentInputBinding uses resolved data ahead of a query parameter with the same input key.
cards.explanation: When route sources share a key, resolved data has the highest precedence for binding that key to a component input.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular uses paramsInheritanceStrategy: 'always' by default for child routes.
cards.explanation: Child routes inherit parent parameters under the default 'always' strategy, including when the parent route has a component.

cards.statement: Angular reactive forms keep an explicitly created form control model in the component's class.
cards.explanation: The component creates the controls that define the form model, giving application code direct access to its value and state.

cards.statement: During change detection, NgModel synchronously applies a new bound model value to its FormControl.
cards.explanation: NgModel queues an asynchronous update when its bound component model changes, rather than immediately setting the internal FormControl.
cards.misconception: NgModel immediately updates its control while Angular checks a changed model binding.

cards.statement: Calling reset() on a FormControl created with new FormControl('Ada') restores the value 'Ada'.
cards.explanation: A FormControl initialized with 'Ada' resets to null when reset() receives no value. With nonNullable: true, it restores its initial value.
cards.misconception: FormControl keeps its initial string as the default reset value.

cards.statement: An enabled FormGroup omits disabled child controls from the value object returned by its value property.
cards.explanation: Disabling a child control removes it from an enabled group's aggregate value, so a typed group's value is Partial.

cards.statement: FormRecord supports a typed collection of controls whose property keys are chosen at runtime.
cards.explanation: FormRecord represents an open set of keys whose controls share a type, making it suitable for dynamically named controls.

cards.statement: Angular's strictly typed forms APIs apply their control-model type checks to template-driven forms.
cards.explanation: The strictly typed controls discussed in Angular's Typed Forms guide apply to reactive forms rather than template-driven forms.
cards.misconception: Strictly typed forms extend their control-model checks to template-driven forms.

cards.statement: In a zoneless application, FormControl.setValue automatically schedules component change detection.
cards.explanation: Reactive form updates change form state and emit form observables, but a zoneless application needs a separate change-detection notification.
cards.misconception: Updating a reactive form model automatically notifies zoneless change detection.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, form() creates a FieldTree whose field structure follows its writable signal model.
cards.explanation: The returned tree exposes fields by model property paths, letting code work with a field's value and state.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, Signal Forms reads an HTML required attribute to add its required validation rule.
cards.explanation: Signal Forms adds required validation through the required() schema function. The form schema supplies the validation rule.
cards.misconception: An HTML required attribute registers a Signal Forms schema validator.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, failed validators stop Signal Forms submit() from running its action by default.
cards.explanation: The default submission options block the action when validators fail. Pending validators alone do not block default submission.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, Signal Forms supports a Map as a structural model container for nested fields.
cards.explanation: Signal Forms builds nested field structure from plain objects and arrays. A Map is not a supported structural container.
cards.misconception: Signal Forms expands Map entries into nested fields like plain object properties.

cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, Angular provides HttpClient for injection through the root injector.
cards.explanation: A default application can inject HttpClient. provideHttpClient customizes its HTTP features.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, HttpClient sends requests through the fetch backend by default.
cards.explanation: Angular selects the fetch backend when HttpClient has no backend override.

cards.statement: Calling HttpClient.get() starts the request as soon as it returns its Observable.
cards.explanation: HttpClient.get() creates a request blueprint. Angular dispatches the request when code subscribes to the returned Observable.
cards.misconception: Creating a HttpClient request Observable immediately sends the request.

cards.statement: By default, subscribers to one HttpClient request Observable share a single backend request.
cards.explanation: HttpClient runs an independent backend request for each subscription to its request Observable.
cards.misconception: HttpClient shares one backend request among subscriptions to the same Observable.

cards.statement: HttpParams.set() updates the original instance that a request's params option references.
cards.explanation: HttpParams.set() returns a new HttpParams instance with the change applied. Pass that returned instance into the request.
cards.misconception: HttpParams mutation methods modify their receiver in place.

cards.statement: withXsrfConfiguration configures the names of HttpClient's XSRF cookie and request header.
cards.explanation: Pass cookieName and headerName to withXsrfConfiguration to match the application's configured XSRF token names.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends functional interceptors over DI-based interceptors.
cards.explanation: Angular recommends functional interceptors because their ordering is more predictable, especially in complex configurations.

cards.statement: HttpClient serializes HttpContext values into outgoing request headers for the server.
cards.explanation: HttpContext stores local request metadata for interceptors. Angular does not send that metadata to the backend.
cards.misconception: HttpContext values become metadata transmitted to the backend.

cards.statement: withRequestsMadeViaParent passes requests through child interceptors before the parent's interceptors.
cards.explanation: The child HttpClient delegates into the parent's HttpClient chain after its own configured interceptors run.

cards.statement: With the fetch backend, HttpClient can emit upload progress events when reportUploadProgress is true.
cards.explanation: Browser upload progress uses withXhr(), reportUploadProgress: true and observe: 'events'. The fetch backend throws if reportUploadProgress is enabled.
cards.misconception: Enabling upload progress works with HttpClient's fetch backend.

cards.statement: After adding @angular/ssr, Angular CLI prerenders application routes by default during a production build.
cards.explanation: Adding @angular/ssr initially configures prerendered pages. Request-time rendering is selected through the server route configuration.

cards.statement: During server rendering, Angular exposes the browser's window global to component constructors.
cards.explanation: The browser's window global is unavailable to component code executing during server rendering.
cards.misconception: Angular supplies browser globals while executing component code on the server.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular creates a fresh value for a top-level useValue provider for each request.
cards.explanation: Top-level useValue values persist across server requests. Angular establishes those values when the application code is first evaluated.
cards.misconception: Angular initializes top-level useValue values separately for incoming server requests.

cards.statement: During prerendering, Angular supplies REQUEST with a Request representing the page being generated.
cards.explanation: REQUEST has the value null during prerendering because that build-time render has no incoming HTTP request.
cards.misconception: Prerendering creates an incoming request object for injection through REQUEST.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular automatically hydrates a component even when its server and client DOM structures differ.
cards.explanation: Hydration expects matching server and client DOM structure, including Angular's generated comments and whitespace.
cards.misconception: Hydration reconciles differing server and client component structures.

cards.statement: In Angular v22.1 with SSR, the transfer cache stores GET requests with withCredentials: true by default.
cards.explanation: Angular's default HTTP transfer cache excludes credential-bearing requests. Setting withCredentials: true makes a request ineligible under that default.
cards.misconception: The default transfer cache includes credential-bearing GET requests.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer-cache eligibility defaults changed in v22.1 and may change in later releases.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, provideClientHydration enables incremental hydration by default with SSR.
cards.explanation: Incremental hydration is part of the hydration provider's default feature set rather than a separate opt-in.
cards.volatilityNote: This hydration default changed in v22 and could be revised in a later major release.

cards.statement: On later client navigation with SSR, Angular loads new @defer views using hydrate triggers.
cards.explanation: Hydrate triggers govern the initial server-rendered load. A new view rendered by later client navigation uses its regular defer triggers.
cards.misconception: Hydrate triggers govern new deferred views during subsequent client navigation.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular keeps nested @defer blocks dehydrated beneath a parent marked `hydrate never` on initial load.
cards.explanation: On the initial server-rendered load, a parent marked hydrate never blocks hydration throughout its nested subtree.

cards.statement: In Angular v22 with SSR, Angular responds to unrecognized Host headers with 400 Bad Request.
cards.explanation: Angular's server pipeline rejects unrecognized hostnames. The allowedHosts option configures which hostnames it accepts.
cards.volatilityNote: Angular's built-in host validation behavior and configuration may evolve in later releases.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends fixture.whenStable() over fixture.detectChanges() in zoneless tests.
cards.explanation: Waiting for stability lets Angular respond to real change notifications. detectChanges() forces a check that the application might not schedule.

cards.statement: ng update leaves source-code migrations to the developer after updating Angular package versions.
cards.explanation: ng update runs applicable migration schematics, which can transform application code as part of the dependency update.
cards.misconception: ng update changes dependency versions while developers perform its code migrations manually.

cards.statement: New Angular CLI applications use the application builder by default for their build system.
cards.explanation: The CLI configures new applications with the stable application builder; existing workspaces may need a migration to adopt it.

cards.statement: With SSR, the application builder requires a separate server builder to compile the application's server code.
cards.explanation: The application builder integrates server compilation with the application build, including configured prerendering.
cards.misconception: The application builder handles client code while a separate builder compiles its SSR server.

cards.statement: Angular CLI uses Vite to bundle application code for an optimized production build.
cards.explanation: Angular uses Vite to serve development builds produced by its build system. The application builder uses esbuild for bundling.
cards.misconception: Angular delegates production application bundling to Vite.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular marks the webpack builders in @angular-devkit/build-angular as deprecated.
cards.explanation: Angular v22 marks @angular-devkit/build-angular's webpack builders as deprecated and directs projects toward @angular/build.
cards.volatilityNote: Deprecated webpack builders may be removed in a future Angular major release.

cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, Angular CLI uses Vitest by default for unit tests in new projects.
cards.explanation: Angular CLI configures a new project's test setup for Vitest when the developer accepts the default runner choice.

cards.statement: Angular's default Vitest setup runs component tests directly in a real browser process.
cards.explanation: Angular's default Vitest setup runs unit tests in Node.js and uses jsdom to simulate browser DOM APIs.
cards.misconception: The default Angular Vitest configuration launches a browser for component tests.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, TestBed uses zoneless change detection by default even when zone.js is loaded.
cards.explanation: Loading zone.js does not choose TestBed's change-detection mode. Its default test environment remains zoneless.

cards.statement: TestBed.createComponent() evaluates template bindings synchronously before returning its fixture.
cards.explanation: TestBed.createComponent() constructs a fixture and component but does not run change detection synchronously to evaluate template bindings.
cards.misconception: Fixture creation completes an initial synchronous template check.

cards.statement: With DeferBlockBehavior.Manual, tests render a @defer block's loading state through its DeferBlockFixture.
cards.explanation: Configure Manual behavior in TestBed, obtain the block fixture, and call render(DeferBlockState.Loading) to select the loading state.
